posts.title: A two-minute brushing routine that actually sticks
posts.excerpt: Two minutes feels long at the sink. Splitting the mouth into four small corners, and giving each one thirty seconds, makes it easy to do well and hard to forget.
posts.content:
Two minutes is the time most dentists suggest for brushing, and it feels surprisingly long when you are standing at the sink. The trick our hygienists teach is to stop thinking about two minutes at all, and think about four corners of thirty seconds each.

Four corners, thirty seconds each

Start at the top right, move to the top left, then the bottom left and the bottom right. In each corner, brush the outside, the inside and the chewing surfaces. When you reach the last corner you are done, and nothing has been skipped.

A small brush, held lightly

Hold the brush like a pen rather than a hammer. Small circles with light pressure clean better than hard scrubbing, and they are kinder to your gums. If the bristles splay out within a month, you are pressing too hard.

  • Use a pea-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste
  • Spit, but try not to rinse straight away
  • Clean between your teeth once a day with floss or small brushes
  • Change your brush every three months, or sooner if it looks tired

Make it part of something you already do

Habits stick when they hang on an existing one. Brush straight after breakfast and just before bed, and keep the floss next to your toothbrush rather than in a drawer. Ask your hygienist at your next visit to show you the one spot your brush tends to miss.

posts.title: How often do you really need a check-up?
posts.excerpt: Every six months is a good rule for most adults, but not for everyone. Here is how we decide, and what actually happens at a check-up.
posts.content:
Many people book a check-up every six months because that is what they have always been told. For most adults it is a sensible rhythm, but the right interval depends on your teeth, your gums and your habits, and it can change over the years.

What happens at a check-up

Your dentist looks at each tooth and at your gums, asks about anything that has changed, and takes X-rays when they are due. A hygienist then cleans and polishes your teeth. It usually takes 30 to 45 minutes.

Why some people come more often

If your gums tend to bleed, if you have had several fillings recently or if you wear a brace, we may suggest every three or four months for a while. If everything has been stable for years, once a year can be enough. Either way, we explain why.

The best check-up is the boring one: nothing new, a quick clean and a reminder for next time.

We send a reminder a few weeks before each check-up is due, by email or by post, whichever you prefer.

posts.title: Your child's first visit: what happens and how to prepare
posts.excerpt: We like to meet children early, before anything needs fixing. A first visit is mostly a game: riding the chair, counting teeth and choosing a sticker.
posts.content:
We like to meet children soon after their first tooth appears, long before anything needs treatment. That way the clinic becomes a familiar place, and the first time a child sits in the chair is not the day they have toothache.

What happens on the day

Your child can sit on your lap or in the big chair, whichever they prefer. We count their teeth out loud, look at their gums with a small mirror and talk with you about brushing and snacks. Most first visits take about twenty minutes.

How to prepare

  • Talk about the visit in a matter-of-fact way, the day before
  • Bring a favourite toy if it helps
  • Book a time of day when your child is usually rested
  • Let us know about anything that worries you, or them

Our Saturday morning sessions are kept for children and families, so the waiting room is full of small people and nobody minds a bit of noise.

posts.title: Sensitive teeth: a few everyday causes worth knowing
posts.excerpt: A sharp twinge with ice cream or a cold drink is common. Often the cause is simple, and small changes help. Sometimes it is worth a closer look.
posts.content:
A short, sharp twinge when you drink something cold is one of the most common things patients mention at a check-up. It is usually harmless, but it is always worth telling your dentist about.

Some everyday causes

  • Brushing too hard, which can wear the gum line
  • Acidic drinks sipped slowly through the day
  • Grinding or clenching at night
  • A small crack or an old filling that needs checking

What can help

A soft brush, a lighter hand and a toothpaste for sensitive teeth help many people. If you grind at night, a thin night guard can protect your teeth. If the twinge lingers, gets worse or wakes you up, book a visit so we can take a look.

This note is general information, not a diagnosis. Your dentist can tell you what is causing your own sensitivity.

posts.title: What is on the tray? The instruments, explained
posts.excerpt: Five instruments, laid out on a pale blue tray at every check-up. Knowing what each one is for takes some of the mystery out of the chair.
posts.content:
Every check-up starts with a fresh tray, opened in front of you. For some people, the instruments are the most worrying part of a visit, so here is what each one does.

The mirror and the probe

The small round mirror lets your dentist see the backs of your teeth. The thin probe checks the surfaces gently and measures the small gap between your teeth and gums.

The scalers

Hygienists use scalers to lift away the hard deposits that brushing cannot reach. You may feel some scraping, but it should not hurt; raise your hand at any time.

Tweezers

For placing and removing small cotton rolls that keep a tooth dry. That is all.

Every instrument is cleaned and sterilised after each patient, and sealed in a pouch until your appointment.

posts.title: Saturday mornings, now every week
posts.excerpt: From September we are open every Saturday from 9:00 to 13:00, with the waiting room kept for children and families.
posts.content:
Many of you have asked for more Saturday appointments, especially for children who are at school during the week. From September we are open every Saturday morning, from 9:00 to 13:00.

Kept for families

Saturday mornings are mostly for children and their parents, with Dr. Rina Ogata and one of our hygienists. Adults are welcome too, but expect a little more noise in the waiting room.

Booking

Saturday slots fill up first, so book a week or two ahead by phone or with the form on our contact page. Thursday afternoons stay closed, as before.
